title: Excessive Wear of Inboard Flap Carriage Rollers Reported by Line Maintenance
abstract: Maintenance organisation reports that the inboard flap carriage rollers wear out well before the published interval on aircraft in high-cycle short-haul operation, and asks for a durable roller and track combination that removes the repeat wear check.

sections.request: We look after around ninety ZEPHYR-22 family aircraft for eleven customers and we are changing inboard flap carriage rollers far more often than the maintenance planning document suggests. On the busiest aircraft we are down to about 4000 flights between roller changes against a nominal 9000, and on two occasions we found the track surface itself pitted, which turns a two-hour roller change into a five-day track replacement. The wear check itself needs the flaps run to full extension and a mirror inspection from below, so it eats a slot on every A check. Our customers are asking why they are paying for a repeat check that we then fail more often than we pass. We would like a roller and track pairing that lasts the published interval in short-haul use, and ideally one that lets the check be dropped altogether.
sections.background: We opened forty-seven work orders against inboard flap carriage rollers in the last two years across the managed fleet, of which nine escalated to track work. The pattern is strongest on aircraft flown at more than four sectors a day and is largely absent from the low-cycle aircraft in the same fleet. We have tried the alternative roller material offered by the vendor with no measurable improvement.
sections.expected_outcome: A roller and track standard that reaches the published wear interval under short-haul utilisation, retrofittable on wing without removing the flap, and supported by a revised maintenance planning interval so the repeat mirror check can be deleted rather than simply relaxed.

type_data.business_justification: Forty-seven roller replacements and nine track replacements in twenty-four months across a managed fleet of ninety aircraft, with an average of 1.4 lost aircraft-days per escalation.
